summary: Specifies a forward error correction scheme based on the Raptor code for delivering data objects reliably. Raptor is a fountain code: the sender can generate as many encoded symbols as needed from the source data, and a receiver can rebuild the original once it has collected enough of them. It is meant for multicast and broadcast delivery.

eli5.summary: Think of a fountain that keeps squirting out puzzle pieces. You do not need any particular piece. Catch enough of them, whichever ones, and you can rebuild the whole picture.

questions: how does raptor fec recover lost packets
what is the fec payload id
subtitle: A fountain code that lets a sender stream endless repair data so receivers can rebuild a file from whatever pieces arrive.

tldr.problem: When one sender delivers an object to many receivers over a lossy network, retransmitting lost packets to each receiver does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: The Raptor code turns each block of source symbols into intermediate symbols and then generates as many XOR-based repair symbols as needed. A receiver can recover the block from any set of encoding symbols only slightly larger than the number of source symbols.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5053 fully specifies the Raptor scheme as FEC Encoding ID 1, including packet formats, parameters, the encoder and an example decoder. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 5053 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2007. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of this Raptor scheme.

sections.title: A Fountain Code for Object Delivery
sections.content:
RFC 5053 specifies a Forward Error Correction (FEC) scheme based on the Raptor code, following the format defined for FEC schemes in RFC 5052. It is a Fully-Specified FEC Scheme with FEC Encoding ID 1, and the code is identical to the one described in 3GPP's MBMS specification.

Raptor is a fountain code: the encoder can generate as many encoding symbols as it needs on the fly from the source symbols of a source block. The decoder can recover the block from any set of encoding symbols only slightly more in number than the number of source symbols.

It is also a systematic code. The original source symbols can be sent unmodified, along with a number of repair symbols. For background on FEC in reliable multicast, the text points to RFC 3453.
sections.eli5: The sender can keep making fresh puzzle pieces forever, and the first pieces it sends are just the original picture cut up. The receiver only needs a few more pieces than the picture has.

sections.title: Payload IDs and Transmission Information
sections.content:
Every packet carries a 4-octet FEC Payload ID: a 16-bit Source Block Number (SBN) saying which block the symbols belong to, and a 16-bit Encoding Symbol ID (ESI) saying which symbols they are.

The receiver also needs the Object Transmission Information (OTI). The mandatory element is the FEC Encoding ID, which MUST be 1. The common elements are the Transfer Length (F), a non-negative integer less than 2^45, and the Encoding Symbol Length (T), less than 2^16. The scheme-specific element is a 4-octet field with the number of source blocks Z (2 octets), the number of sub-blocks N (1 octet) and the symbol alignment parameter Al (1 octet). The full encoded OTI is 14 octets.
sections.eli5: Each packet has a small label saying which puzzle it belongs to and which pieces are inside. A separate cover sheet tells the receiver how big the puzzle is and how it was cut.

sections.title: Parameters from the Content Delivery Protocol
sections.content:
The Raptor scheme relies on a Content Delivery Protocol (CDP) to carry its information. The encoder and decoder need the transfer length F in bytes, the alignment parameter Al, the symbol size T (which MUST be a multiple of Al), the number of source blocks Z and the number of sub-blocks N. For each packet the encoder hands the CDP the SBN, the ESI and the encoding symbols, and the CDP MUST communicate these to the receiver.

The RFC also gives an example algorithm to derive T, Z and N from the object size F, a sub-block size target W, the maximum packet payload P, Al, and limits Kmin and Gmax. The recommended settings are Al = 4, Kmin = 1024 and Gmax = 10. Choosing Al so that symbol sizes are multiples of the machine word size speeds up the XOR operations. The W parameter lets a decoder work with limited memory.
sections.eli5: Whoever delivers the puzzle must tell the receiver how big the pieces are and how many sections the puzzle has. The RFC gives a recipe for picking those numbers.

sections.title: Source Blocks, Symbols and Packets
sections.content:
An object is split into Z source blocks, each encoded independently and numbered from zero. Each block holds K source symbols of T bytes, and K can be at most Kmax = 8192. Parameters MUST satisfy ceil(ceil(F/T)/Z) <= Kmax. If the last symbol is short, it is padded with zero bytes for encoding.

A block can also be divided into N sub-blocks small enough to decode in working memory, and a symbol is built from one sub-symbol of each sub-block. With N greater than 1, a symbol is therefore not a contiguous part of the object.

ESIs from 0 to K-1 identify the source symbols; ESIs from K onwards identify repair symbols. A packet holds either only source symbols or only repair symbols, all from one block. The receiver does not need to know the total number of repair packets.
sections.eli5: A big puzzle is cut into smaller puzzles, each solved on its own. The first pieces are the real picture, and every piece after that is an extra helper piece.

sections.title: The Systematic Raptor Encoder
sections.content:
Encoding has two steps. First, the K source symbols are turned into L intermediate symbols with L = K + S + H, where S is a number of LDPC symbols and H a number of Half symbols. These satisfy fixed pre-coding relationships, and are found by an inverse encoding process, which can be run as a decoder. Intermediate symbols are never sent in packets.

Second, each repair symbol is the XOR of several intermediate symbols, picked by a triple (d, a, b) from the Triple generator for that symbol's ESI. The degree d is drawn from a fixed table where degree 1 covers a small share of values, degrees 2 to 4 most of the rest, and the largest degree is 40. The pseudo-random generator uses two tables, V0 and V1, of 256 four-byte integers each, which MUST be available to both sender and receiver. A table of systematic indices J(K) covers block sizes from 4 to 8192 source symbols.
sections.eli5: The sender first mixes the picture pieces into a secret blend. Each new helper piece is then made by combining a few ingredients from that blend, in a way both sides can repeat exactly.

sections.title: Decoding a Source Block
sections.content:
The RFC specifies the encoder; it says several decoding algorithms are possible and gives an efficient example. Each received encoding symbol is an equation among the intermediate symbols. With N received symbols (at least K), the decoder forms a bit matrix over GF(2) and solves it for the intermediate symbols, which succeeds if and only if the matrix has rank L.

The example decoder uses Gaussian elimination in phases, with a carefully chosen row order for speed. The order does not affect whether decoding succeeds, but it affects speed a great deal, and a sparse matrix representation is crucial. Once the intermediate symbols are known, any missing source symbols are recovered using their triples. Padding bytes that were left out of a packet must be reinserted before decoding.
sections.eli5: The receiver treats every piece it caught as a clue and solves all the clues together. Once the blend is recovered, any missing picture pieces can be re-made.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Corrupted packets that receivers accept as legitimate can enable denial of service, especially in multicast, where a bad packet injected near the root of the tree reaches many receivers. Because of the way the code works, even one corrupted encoding packet can make the decoded object completely corrupted and unusable.

The RFC therefore RECOMMENDS source authentication and integrity checking of decoded objects, for example appending a SHA-1 hash, with a digital signature SHOULD be provided. It also RECOMMENDS a packet authentication protocol such as TESLA (RFC 4082), and Reverse Path Forwarding checks in routers and switches. Because FEC information may come from a session description, receivers should only accept descriptions from authorized senders.
sections.eli5: One fake puzzle piece can ruin the whole picture, so receivers should check that the pieces and the finished picture are genuine.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The RFC assigns the Fully-Specified FEC Encoding ID 1 under the ietf:rmt:fec:encoding name-space to "Raptor Code". General IANA guidance for FEC schemes is in RFC 5052.
sections.eli5: The number 1 is now officially reserved as the name tag for this way of making puzzle pieces.
